nameStory: The Lesser Yellowlegs gets its name from its bright yellow-orange legs that really stand out against its gray and white body. The 'lesser' part distinguishes it from its larger cousin, the Greater Yellowlegs, which looks remarkably similar but is noticeably bigger with a longer, slightly upturned bill.
description: The Lesser Yellowlegs is a graceful, medium-sized shorebird about the size of a robin, standing on long, bright yellow legs. Its body is mottled gray-brown above with white below, and it has a straight, thin dark bill that's perfect for picking insects and small fish from shallow water. During migration, you'll often see these elegant waders stepping carefully through mudflats and marsh edges, their heads bobbing as they search for food.

idTips.label: Bright yellow legs
idTips.description: Vivid yellow-orange legs that look almost like they're wearing bright socks - much more colorful than most other shorebirds

idTips.label: Straight, thin bill
idTips.description: Dark bill that's straight as a needle and about the same length as the head, perfect for precise picking at small prey

idTips.label: Gray and white plumage
idTips.description: Mottled gray-brown back with clean white underparts, giving it a neat, well-pressed appearance

idTips.label: Bobbing behavior
idTips.description: Constantly bobs its head and rear end while walking, like it's keeping time to music only it can hear

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: About robin-sized with a slender build, noticeably smaller and more delicate than most other long-legged shorebirds

habitat: Look for Lesser Yellowlegs along mudflats, shallow pond edges, salt marshes, and flooded fields throughout New England during migration. They prefer areas where the water is just ankle-deep, allowing them to wade comfortably while hunting for small fish, insects, and crustaceans. You'll often spot them at places like Plum Island in Massachusetts or the Connecticut River estuary.

seasonality.spring: Migrants pass through in April and May, often in small flocks, as they head to their northern breeding grounds. Look for them in fresh spring plumage with crisp markings.
seasonality.summer: Very few remain in New England during breeding season, as most continue north to Canada's boreal forests. Any summer sightings are likely non-breeding birds or early fall migrants.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration time from July through September, when both adults and juveniles pass through. Young birds show especially neat, organized feather patterns.
seasonality.winter: Occasionally a few hardy individuals winter along the coast, particularly in southern New England, though most continue to warmer southern regions.

funFact: Lesser Yellowlegs can actually swim when they need to! While they prefer to wade in shallow water, they'll dive completely underwater to escape predators and can paddle around like little ducks until the danger passes.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Greater Yellowlegs, but remember the rhyme: 'Lesser legs, lesser length' - the Lesser has a shorter bill (about head-length) and smaller overall size. The Greater's bill is noticeably longer and often has a slight upward curve, while the Lesser's is perfectly straight.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'yellowlegs,' their leg color can actually fade to pale orange or even dull yellow depending on lighting and season. Don't let this throw you off - the legs are still much brighter than any other similar-sized shorebird you'll see in New England.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Greater Yellowlegs, the Lesser is noticeably smaller with a shorter, always-straight bill. Unlike the Solitary Sandpiper (another Tringa relative), Lesser Yellowlegs prefer open mudflats over secluded woodland pools. The Willet, while also having yellowish legs, is much bulkier and shows dramatic black-and-white wing patterns in flight that the Lesser lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tringa relatives, Greater Yellowlegs is larger than Lesser Yellowlegs and Solitary Sandpiper, with brighter yellow legs than either.
Among its Tringa relatives, the willet dwarfs both greater and lesser yellowlegs with its robust build and lacks their bright yellow legs entirely.
Compared to its Tringa cousins, the Solitary Sandpiper is smaller than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs with much darker, greenish legs instead of bright yellow ones.
Wood Sandpiper is much smaller and more delicate than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs, with proportionally shorter legs and bill.
Compared to its New England relatives in the same genus, the Common Redshank is smaller than Greater Yellowlegs but similar in size to Lesser Yellowlegs, though much stockier in build.
Compared to its New England cousins, the spotted redshank has the brightest colored legs - much more vivid red-orange than the yellow of both yellowlegs species.
